Where it began

Geoffrey Boycott was born on 21 October 1940 in Fitzwilliam, a mining village near Wakefield. He learned the game in its terraced streets, with a manhole cover for a wicket, and he always reckoned that was where his favourite strokes came from: the square cut, the clip off his legs and the straight drive, which on that street could run all the way to the bottom.

He joined Ackworth Cricket Club at ten and captained his grammar school at 15. When his eyesight faded in his teens he took the field in spectacles, later swapping them for contact lenses. He was a useful footballer too, turning out for the Leeds United under-18 side alongside Billy Bremner, and after leaving school he worked as a clerk in Barnsley while playing club cricket for Barnsley next to Dickie Bird and Michael Parkinson.

The player

Yorkshire gave him his debut in 1962 and England followed in 1964, against Australia at Trent Bridge. He made his first Test hundred at The Oval that summer and was one of Wisden's Cricketers of the Year in 1965. He played 108 Tests between 1964 and 1982 and made 8,114 runs at 47.73, with 22 hundreds and 42 fifties. His highest score, an unbeaten 246, came against India at Headingley in 1967.

Two moments stand out. Returning to the side in 1977, he batted on all five days of the Trent Bridge Test, and later that summer, at Headingley in front of his own crowd, he made 191 against Australia and became the first man to reach his hundredth first-class century in a Test. Then, in India in the winter of 1981–82, he passed Gary Sobers to become the leading run-scorer in Test history.

What made him special

Concentration was his great gift. He could bat for hours, and England relied on it: they never lost a Test in which he made a hundred. In English first-class cricket he twice averaged over 100 for a season, in 1971 and 1979, the first English player ever to manage it, and he went past Len Hutton's record of 129 first-class hundreds.

Speed was not his first concern, and one-day cricket suited him less. Yet he could cut loose when he chose: his 146 against Surrey won Yorkshire the Gillette Cup final of 1965. His bowling brought him seven Test wickets, which for a man so careful with his own wicket seems only polite.

Away from the middle

He was made an OBE for his services to cricket and was later knighted, becoming Sir Geoffrey. After he stopped playing he became a well-known voice on radio and television, part of the Test Match Special team until he retired in 2020, and he claimed credit for the phrase "corridor of uncertainty". The singer Roy Harper dedicated the song When An Old Cricketer Leaves The Crease to him and John Snow.

And finally

At Perth in December 1978 he made 77 without hitting a single boundary, the highest score of its kind. There was one four in it, though. He ran all of it.
